title: Shadowgate: The Living Castle - a review from a solo perspective
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7BXf6nTyiCQ

Shadowgate: The Living Castle (review copy from Trick or Treat Studios) adapts the 1987 MacVenture point-and-click game, and Daniel (@dungeondive) starts with the history. ICOM Simulations swapped the text parser for mouse-driven commands. He played Uninvited and Déjà Vu on the Macintosh, and he remembers wrestling King's Quest's syntax to kill a snake. Then a tangent: Shadowgate characters come from a 1991 Worlds of Power novel, and his own Blaster Master volume ends with a reading list for kids that runs from Jules Verne to A Wrinkle in Time.

In the board game, players compete for XP while jointly working through four tiers of quest decks toward a final boss: the Behemoth, the Reaper or the Warlock Lord. He admires how puzzle items recreate adventure-game backtracking. Each item names the deck its puzzle lives in, so you can cycle quests to get back to that locked library. There's also a torch track that spawns curses, death cards costing five points, genie riddles, and clever choices between equipping, spending or banking cards for points. Zojoi's art and the flavour text are excellent.

But it plays as a thematic competitive card game, not an adventure; he compares it to the Dark Souls and Bloodborne card games. Played solo or two-handed, the take-that combos fall flat, and he wished he had opponents. He has had fun, but he can't recommend it for solo play and wants to try it with friends.

----

Did you play the MacVenture games (Shadowgate, Uninvited, Déjà Vu) back in the day? Can a card game capture what made them memorable?
